title: Change Blindness
summary: Find the single difference between two versions of a street scene. Run the same scene again with the blank between them switched off, and compare the two searches.
learningObjectives: Explain what the blank interval does to the local transient produced by a change.
Predict and check how much easier the same change becomes without a blank.
Describe how change type, position and size affect the search.
Explain why change blindness does not show that people store nothing about a scene.
Recognise that a slow search is time spent looking elsewhere, not time spent blind.
interactionTypes: transparent reveal with the change ringed
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; search times and answers stay in the browser tab, nothing is written to storage, and the record of which scenes have been revealed is a JavaScript variable that disappears on reload.
accessibilityNotes: The alternation is deliberately slow: a full cycle is 1.7 seconds (600 ms per view, 250 ms per blank), so the screen changes about 1.2 times a second - well below the three-per-second threshold associated with photosensitive reactions, and much slower than the standard laboratory paradigm. A Pause button is available throughout, and a manual-stepping mode advances only on a button press or the space bar. Under prefers-reduced-motion the tool starts in manual mode and says so in the live region; the phenomenon depends on the blank rather than the speed, so nothing is lost. No CSS animation or transition is used anywhere. Scene parts are distinguished by fill and outline, and the change is always geometric or a lit/unlit state rather than a hue, so the task works in greyscale and in forced colours. The live scene is aria-hidden because describing it aloud would state the answer; the reveal names the change in words and rings it with a dashed circle. Every control has an accessible name; headings do not skip; focus moves to the results heading. Usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: Change blindness: what the blank interval does, and what it does not show
simulationNotes: The scenes are original vector drawings generated deterministically from fixed seeds (20260911 to 20260914): a sky, a sun, three clouds, four buildings with grids of lit and unlit windows, three trees and a fence. Nothing is derived from a photograph or any other source. Four trials vary the change on three declared dimensions - a whole tree removed (presence, centre, large); one window's light flipped (state, right edge, small); a building's height raised by an extra storey (size, left edge, large); a cloud moved 96 units sideways (position, upper centre, medium). Those three properties are declared rather than manipulated factorially: with one scene each they are completely confounded with each other and with the scene, and the trial table says so in those words rather than inviting a comparison the design cannot support. The one comparison the design does support is the same scene with and without the blank. Times are the learner's own, in a browser, at an uncontrolled scene size, with an alternation slower than the published paradigm, so they are not comparable with published figures and measure nothing about the person. Each scene works properly once; the tool marks revealed scenes and keeps that record across a reset.
